course.title: Logic and Reasoning
course.description: Work out what follows from what. Read arguments carefully, test them against cases, and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong.
course.audience: A general reader with no background in formal logic who wants to argue and evaluate arguments more carefully.

paragraphs: Logic is the study of what follows from what. A conclusion either follows from the reasons offered for it or it doesn't, and logic gives you ways to tell which. People study it to read arguments more carefully, and to see where everyday reasoning goes wrong. It is also the rule-following side of mathematics and computing, so it helps with both.

The course has eight lessons in two parts. The first part, Deduction, begins with sentences that can be true or false. It then covers if-then rules and how to turn one round, a puzzle that you solve by trying each case, and the truth table, which lists every case at once. The second part, Arguments, takes an argument in everyday words and picks out its conclusion and its reasons. It then separates a valid argument from a sound one and names the common ways reasoning fails.
Each lesson tells you the idea first and asks questions afterwards, so you meet a question only once you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a claim from a question or a command, and say what its truth value is.
You'll be able to say exactly when an if-then rule is broken, and write its converse and its contrapositive.
You'll be able to solve a knights and knaves puzzle by trying each case and ruling out the ones that break a rule.
You'll be able to build a truth table for two claims and use it to test a piece of reasoning.
You'll be able to pick out the conclusion of an argument, tell valid from sound, and name the common fallacies.
introduction.prerequisites: You don't need any background in logic or mathematics, only the habit of reading a sentence carefully.

modules.title: Deduction
modules.description: What it means for a conclusion to follow from its premises, and how to test whether it does.

modules.title: Arguments
modules.description: Telling a good argument from a persuasive one, and naming the ways reasoning fails.

concepts.title: Statement
concepts.summary: A sentence that is either true or false, which is what logic operates on.

concepts.title: Conditional
concepts.summary: An if-then claim, which is false only when the antecedent holds and the consequent fails.

concepts.title: Truth table
concepts.summary: An exhaustive listing of the cases a compound statement can take.

concepts.title: Negation and converse
concepts.summary: Turning a conditional around or inside out changes what it claims.

concepts.title: Premise and conclusion
concepts.summary: The claims offered as support, and the claim they are meant to support.

concepts.summary: Whether the conclusion follows, and separately whether the premises are true.

concepts.title: Fallacy
concepts.summary: A pattern of reasoning that persuades without supporting.

lessons.title: What logic operates on

lead.text: Go back to the envelope. Mia's sentence, “It holds a £10 note”, says how things are. That makes it something anyone could check. Open the envelope and either she was right or she was wrong. A sentence like that is called a claim.

Not every sentence works this way. “Is there a note in the envelope?” asks for information. It can be answered, but it can't be right or wrong in the way Mia's sentence can. “Open the envelope” is a command, and a command can be obeyed or ignored without ever being wrong. Only a sentence that says how things are can turn out to be wrong.

That gives the first skill in logic, which is sorting. Faced with a sentence, ask whether it says how things are. If it does, it is a claim and there is something to test. If it asks or tells, it is a different kind of sentence and there is nothing to test.

diagram.caption: Sentences sorted by what they do. Only the ones that say how things are can turn out to be wrong.

lead.text: A lamp stands in a corner of the room. A sentence about it can say how it is, ask about it or tell someone what to do with it.

Back to Mia and Jon. Mia's claim is waiting for a verdict, and the verdict comes from checking the claim against how things are. If the envelope holds a £10 note, her claim passes. If it holds anything else, or nothing, her claim fails. That verdict is the claim's truth value, and the two values on offer are true and false.

Look at who sets the verdict. The envelope does. Nobody has opened it, but it still holds exactly what it holds, so Mia's claim already has a truth value. All that is missing is anyone knowing it. Calling a claim “unknown” describes what we have found out so far, and the claim itself already has one value. A third value never joins the list.

So in any real situation a claim has exactly one truth value, and that value is one of two. Jon's sentence, “It doesn't”, is the other side of the same envelope. Whichever way the envelope turns out, one of the two sentences passes and the other fails.

lead.text: Mia's claim is waiting for a verdict and nobody has looked. Think about which verdicts a claim can end up with, then count them.

reveal.text: Two: true and false. If you were tempted to count “unknown”, remember that the word describes what we know. The envelope still holds what it holds.

lead.text: Put Jon's sentence next to Mia's. Jon's sentence is Mia's claim with “not” put in, and it says that her claim fails. Logic has a name and a symbol for that move.

Writing out whole sentences gets tedious, so a claim is given a short name, usually the letter p. If p is “The lamp is on”, then ¬p is “The lamp is not on”. The symbol ¬ reads “not”, and ¬p is called the negation of p. It is a claim in its own right, so it has a truth value of its own.

The envelope shows how the two values are related. Mia's claim and Jon's are negations of each other, and they can't both pass or both fail. Whichever way the envelope is, one of them is right and the other wrong. That is what the next screen asks you to work out for the lamp.
Suppose p is “The lamp is on”, and the lamp is on.

reveal.text: The table shows both rows, and your answer matches the first one: negation turns each value into the other.

lead.text: A claim doesn't have to be easy to settle. The envelope can be opened in a moment, but some claims are hard to check and some are argued about for years. Two people can disagree sharply about whether a soup is too salty, and nobody calls the sentence “This soup is too salty” a question or a command.

What makes it a claim is that the speaker says how something is. Whether anyone can settle the matter, and whether anyone agrees, comes afterwards. The same holds for a claim about something hidden, such as a coin under a cup. A claim about something nobody has measured yet works the same way. Each is checked against how things are, and each has a truth value whether or not we can find it.

Logic does not decide matters of taste or fill in missing information. It starts from sentences that say how things are, and it asks what follows once their truth values are fixed. The last screen of the lesson tests the sorting on a sentence that people dispute.
Two friends argue about a painting. One says: “This painting is beautiful.” The other disagrees.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish truth-apt claims from questions and commands, including claims whose truth is unknown or disputed.
lessons.nextAction: A claim can be true or false, even when its truth is unknown.

blocks.text: Mia and Jon are arguing over a sealed envelope. Mia says: “It holds a £10 note.” Jon says: “It doesn't.” Nobody has opened it, so nobody can say who is right, and the argument goes round in circles for a while.

Anyone listening can tell something is odd about it. Mia and Jon are both talking about what is in the envelope, and the envelope isn't saying anything. It holds a note or it doesn't, and that was settled when someone sealed it. They are arguing about a fact that already exists and that neither of them knows.

Logic starts with sentences like theirs. First we sort out which sentences can be wrong at all. Then we look at what it means that nobody has looked yet, and at how to state the opposite of a sentence. The lesson ends with a sentence that people argue about even though there is nothing to open.

intro.whyItMatters: Arguments are built from claims, so spotting one is the first step to testing an argument.

recap.keyIdea: Logic works on claims. In any situation a claim has exactly one truth value, whether or not anyone knows it. Negation reverses that value.

blocks.text: Back at the sealed envelope, you decided that it already holds what it holds, so Mia's claim already has an answer. You flipped a claim with negation and saw that a lamp that is on makes “the lamp is not on” false. You also saw that a claim people argue about, like “This painting is beautiful”, is still a claim.

lessons.title: If-then claims

steps.headline: The two halves of a promise

lead.text: Look at Sam's sentence again: “If you pass your test, I'll buy you lunch.” It has two halves joined by “if … then”. A sentence of that shape is called a conditional, because what Sam does depends on something else happening first.

The half after “if” is the antecedent: you pass your test. The half after “then” is the consequent: Sam buys you lunch. The antecedent sets the condition, and the consequent says what follows when the condition is met.

Each half is a claim in its own right, so each can be true or false. That lets us use the short names from the last lesson. Call the antecedent p and the consequent q, and write the whole sentence as p → q, with the arrow reading “if … then”. The order matters. In p → q the condition always comes first, and the rest of the lesson depends on telling the two halves apart.

diagram.caption: Sam's promise as p → q. The condition comes first and the arrow points to what follows.

steps.headline: When a promise can be broken

lead.text: A promise can only be broken in a situation it covers. Sam's covers the situation where you pass, and in that situation there are two possibilities. You pass and Sam buys the lunch, so he has kept his word. You pass and Sam doesn't buy the lunch, so he has broken it.

Notice what the broken case needs. The condition has been met, because you passed, and the result is missing, because there was no lunch. A condition that is met is what puts the promise to the test, and a missing result is what fails the test.
That covers the days when you pass. It leaves the days when you fail the test, and the promise has to be read carefully there. The next few screens take it case by case.

lead.text: Let p mean “The access code is correct” and q mean “The door opens.” The rule p → q is a promise from the door.

reveal.text: Compare your choice with the one case where the code is right and the door stays shut. That is Sam's pass-and-no-lunch again, with a door in place of Sam.

lead.text: Now the days the promise doesn't cover. You fail the test, and Sam buys lunch anyway. He promised lunch if you passed, and you didn't pass, so the condition was never met. Whatever Sam does now, he hasn't gone against what he said. Buying you lunch is a generous extra, and it contradicts nothing.

The same goes for the day when you fail and Sam buys no lunch. He said nothing about that day either, and nobody can accuse him of breaking a promise that didn't apply. On both days the promise is untouched. In logic we call the conditional true in those cases, meaning that it has not been broken.

That is a convention, and it helps to state it plainly. A conditional gets the value false when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false. When the antecedent is false, the conditional is true whatever the consequent does.

diagram.alt: Two outcomes on a day you fail the test. Sam buys lunch anyway, or buys none. In both the promise is untouched.

p and q can each be true or false, which makes four cases in all. You have now decided what the rule says in every one of them.

Here are the four cases side by side. Each row says whether p and q are true, and the last column says whether p → q is true in that row. A list of every case with the result beside each is how logicians check anything that depends on a few claims, and the course uses it a lot.

afterFigure.text: Read the table with Sam in mind. Only the second row is false, and it is the pass-and-no-lunch row. The other three are true, and two of them are rows where the condition was never met. A false antecedent hands you a true conditional automatically.

One mistake to watch for is reading a true consequent as a sign that the antecedent was true. In the third row q is true and p is false. A lunch bought on a day you failed says nothing about whether you passed.

lead.text: Take the rule “If a shape is a square, it has four sides.” A rectangle with four sides turns up. It isn't a square.

lessons.orientation: State exactly when a conditional is false, and resist the pull to read it as a promise about the antecedent.
lessons.nextAction: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.

blocks.text: Sam says to you: “If you pass your test, I'll buy you lunch.” The test comes and you fail. A week later Sam turns up and buys you lunch anyway.

It is tempting to say that something odd has happened, as if the promise had been quietly swapped for a different one. People disagree about this. Some say Sam broke his promise by giving you something you hadn't earned. Others say he kept it. Settling it means finding out exactly what the promise covers.

Sentences built with “if … then” turn up in rules, in laws and in the small print of every prize draw, and a mistake in reading them is easy to make. This lesson takes Sam's promise apart and lists everything that can happen to it. One situation turns out to break it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the one case that breaks an if-then rule, and see why a failed condition never breaks it.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional p → q is false in exactly one case: p true and q false. Every other case leaves it true.

blocks.text: Back to Sam: failing the test and getting lunch anyway breaks nothing, because the promise only covers the case where you pass. You found the one case that breaks the door's rule, and you showed that a four-sided rectangle that isn't a square leaves “If it's a square, it has four sides” untouched.

recap.nextHook: Sam's promise runs from passing to lunch. The next lesson turns a rule round to see whether the version that runs the other way says the same thing.

lessons.title: Converse and contrapositive

lead.text: Take the policy as it stands. “If a file is encrypted, then it needs a key” has the form p → q, with p for “the file is encrypted” and q for “the file needs a key”. The condition comes first and what follows from it comes second.

Turning a rule round can mean several things, and the simplest is to swap the two halves. That gives “If a file needs a key, then it is encrypted”, which is q → p. A rule made by swapping the antecedent and consequent like this is called the converse of the original.

People often treat the converse as if it were the same rule said differently. The first colleague did exactly that. Whether it says the same thing is what the next few screens test, and the test is simple: look for a case in which the two disagree.

steps.headline: How to tell two rules apart

lead.text: Two rules say the same thing only if they are true together and false together in every possible case. That gives a way to compare them. Write down every case, work out each rule in it, and look for a case where one is true and the other false. A single case like that is enough to show that the rules differ.

Try the case where the file is encrypted and does need a key, so p and q are both true. The original, p → q, is true, because the condition is met and the result follows. The converse, q → p, is true as well, because its condition q is met and its result p follows. Here the two agree, and that proves nothing, since rules can agree in one case and still differ in another.

So agreement in one case settles nothing, while disagreement in one case settles everything. To tell the converse from the original we need a case where they come apart. The next screen tries a file that needs a key without being encrypted.

reveal.text: Your answer shows a case where the original holds and the converse fails. The two rules disagree, so the converse is a different claim. The second colleague was right.

lead.text: Swapping alone changed the meaning, so look for a way of turning the rule round that keeps it. The idea is to run the reasoning backwards. If every encrypted file needs a key, then a file with no key can't be encrypted, because had it been encrypted it would have needed one.

Written out, that is “If a file doesn't need a key, then it isn't encrypted”, which is ¬q → ¬p. Two things were done to the original. The halves were swapped, as for the converse, and each half was negated, using the ¬ from the first lesson. A rule built this way is called the contrapositive of the original.

It is worth checking that this one says the same thing, and the check is the one from before: go through the cases and compare. The next screen does the first two cases for you and leaves the other two to you.

lead.text: Both rules need to be worked out in each case. Write ¬q and ¬p first, and then read the rule from them.

p true, q false. The original has a true condition and a missing result, so it is false. In the other rule ¬q is true and ¬p is false, so it is false too.

lead.text: The worked example covered the two cases where p is true. Do the two where p is false in the same way, then look across all four cases.

steps.headline: What the contrapositive lets you conclude

lead.text: Because the contrapositive says the same thing, it gives a second way to use any rule. “If a file is encrypted, it needs a key” has the contrapositive “If a file doesn't need a key, it isn't encrypted”. A file that opens without a key must be unencrypted, and the engineer can say so with confidence.

The opposite finding gives no such confidence. A file that needs a key tells you nothing certain, because the converse, “If a file needs a key, it is encrypted”, is a different rule that nobody has said holds. The colleague who said the file must be encrypted was reading the converse into the policy. The other colleague had it right.
Of the two ways to turn a rule round, only one keeps its meaning. Swap the halves and negate both, and the meaning stays. Swap them and leave them alone, and the meaning changes.
A courier's rule: “If a parcel is fragile, then it gets a warning label.”

lessons.orientation: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.
lessons.nextAction: Solve a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it to a contradiction.

blocks.text: A company's security policy says: “If a file is encrypted, then it needs a key to open.” That is the whole rule. An engineer finds a file on the shared drive and discovers that it needs a key to open.

One colleague says the file must be encrypted, since the policy ties encryption to keys. Another says the policy allows no such conclusion. They are reading the same sentence, and only one of them can be right.

Both colleagues are turning the rule round, which people do all the time with rules and promises. There are two common ways to do it. This lesson tests each one against every case, and finds which one says the same thing as the original and which one says something new.

intro.promise: By the end you'll write the converse and contrapositive of an if-then rule, and know which one says the same thing.

recap.keyIdea: A conditional says the same thing as its contrapositive, ¬q → ¬p. It does not say the same thing as its converse, q → p.

blocks.text: Back on the shared drive, you found that a file needing a key need not be encrypted. You checked all four cases and found none where p → q and ¬q → ¬p disagree. You also wrote the contrapositive of a courier's rule about fragile parcels.

recap.nextHook: You can now turn a rule round without changing what it says. The next lesson takes that care to a puzzle on an island where some people always lie.

lessons.title: Knights and knaves

steps.headline: What each kind of islander can say

lead.text: The whole puzzle rests on two rules. A knight's statement is always true, and a knave's statement is always false. That holds for everything they say, so a knave can never say “Two plus two is four”, because that is true. A knave can't say a true thing by accident.

The rules link what a person is to what their sentence is worth. If you know someone is a knight, you can believe what they say. If you know someone is a knave, you can believe the negation of what they say. The puzzle runs the link the other way: from what people say, work out what they are.

steps.headline: Assuming a case and following it

lead.text: Suppose Cleo says: “Dan is a knight.” We know nothing about either of them yet, so start by assuming something. Assume Cleo is a knight. Her sentence is then true, which means Dan is a knight.

Now assume the opposite, that Cleo is a knave. Her sentence is then false, so Dan is not a knight, which makes him a knave. Both assumptions led somewhere sensible. Neither one broke a rule, so neither could be thrown out.

That is the method in outline. Choose a type for the speaker, see what their sentence then forces on everyone else, and check that nobody has been made to say something that doesn't fit their type. When a choice forces someone to break their rule, it can't be the real situation.

Two assumptions were enough for Cleo, but with several people we need a tidier way to keep track. A choice of knight or knave for each person is called an assignment. For Cleo and Dan there are four. Both can be knights, or both knaves. Cleo can be a knight with Dan a knave, or the other way round.

Go through the assignments one at a time and check Cleo's sentence, “Dan is a knight”, against each. With both knights, her sentence is true and she is a knight, which is fine. With Cleo a knight and Dan a knave, her sentence is false, which a knight can't say. With Cleo a knave and Dan a knight, her sentence is true, which a knave can't say. With both knaves, her sentence is false, which suits a knave.

An assignment that makes someone break the rule for their type is a contradiction, and it is ruled out. Cleo's sentence rules out two assignments and leaves two. A single sentence often leaves several standing, because it never says which one holds. With two people there are 2 × 2 = 4 assignments to test, and a third person would double that.

lead.text: Ada's sentence left two assignments. Now Ben speaks too. Test each of the two against his sentence.

Every sentence works as a filter. Ada's removed two assignments, and Ben's removed one of the two that were left. When exactly one assignment survives, that is the answer. When several survive, the sentences leave the matter open and you need more information.

A third outcome is possible. If every assignment makes somebody break their rule, none survives and the puzzle has no solution. No pair of islanders of these two kinds could have said what was said. The method has not failed when this happens. It has shown that the sentences contradict each other.

blocks.text: On a small island everyone is either a knight or a knave. Knights always tell the truth. Knaves always lie. You can't tell by looking which kind a person is, and the only way to find out is to listen to what they say.

Two islanders, Ada and Ben, stand in front of you. Ada says: “Ben is a knave.” That single sentence doesn't settle who is who, but it does rule some possibilities out. If she is a knight, her sentence has to be true. If she is a knave, it has to be false. Each choice leads somewhere different, and following them is how this kind of puzzle gets solved.

The method is general. You pick a possibility, follow it through everything the islanders say, and throw it out if it breaks a rule. This lesson builds the method on Ada and Ben and then tries it on pairs that are harder to read.

lessons.title: Building a truth table

lead.text: Treat the lamps as two claims. Let p be “Lamp 1 is on” and let q be “Lamp 2 is on”. Each lamp is on or off, so p is true or false and q is true or false. A state of the hallway is a choice of true or false for both, written with two letters. TT means both lamps are on, and TF means lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is off.

To list every state without gaps, fix lamp 1 first and pair it with both settings of lamp 2, then do the same with lamp 1 off. That gives four rows: TT, TF, FT and FF. Two choices for the first lamp, each paired with two for the second, make 2 × 2 rows. Each extra lamp would double the list. A list that skips a pairing, or repeats one, is wrong.

afterFigure.text: A list of every row, with the value of a sentence beside each, is called a truth table. The one above gives the value of “If lamp 1 is on, then lamp 2 is on”, which is p → q, the conditional from the if-then lesson. It is false in a single row. The rest of the lesson builds tables for two other sentences.

diagram.outputLabel: If lamp 1 is on, lamp 2 is on

lead.text: The hallway has two lamps, and each one is either on or off.

steps.headline: Testing a sentence in every row

lead.text: A table earns its keep when you ask it about a sentence. Take “Lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is on”. In symbols that is p ∧ q, where ∧ reads “and”. The sentence is a claim, so each row gives it a truth value, and to find the value you ask whether the sentence describes the state in that row correctly.

Go row by row. The row TT describes lamps that are both on, so the sentence describes it correctly. For each of the other rows, check the two lamps in turn against the sentence, which needs both of them. Doing this for all four rows fills in a column of values, one for each state. The sentence stays the same from row to row, and only the state it is checked against changes.
The symbol ∧ reads “and”: p ∧ q says that p holds and q holds. Go through the four rows and test it in each.

reveal.text: Compare your count with the table. Only TT survives, because each other row leaves one claim false.

lead.text: The word “or” is slipperier than “and”. A café sign says “Tea or coffee included with breakfast”, and nobody expects to be turned away for taking both. A menu that says “soup or salad” usually means one or the other, and you are expected to choose. The same word is doing two jobs.

Logic settles this once. The symbol ∨ reads “or” and includes the case where both claims hold. The claim p ∨ q is true when at least one of p and q is true, and that includes the case where both are. This reading is called the inclusive or. The other one rules out taking both. It is called exclusive, and we won't use it unless we say so.
Fixing the meaning matters because a table only works when each symbol reads the same way every time. With ∨ settled, any table that uses it can be read the same way.

steps.headline: Using the rows to test reasoning

lead.text: Rows can do more than evaluate a sentence. They can test a piece of reasoning. Suppose we are told two things about p and q and asked what follows. Each row is a possible state of the world, and the facts we are told rule out some of them.

Here is the method with different facts. We know that p ∧ q is false and that p is true. List the four rows. Keep only the rows where p ∧ q is false, which are TF, FT and FF. Then keep only the rows where p is true. That leaves TF, and in TF the claim q is false. In every row that fits what we know, q is false, so q must be false.
The same table also catches bad reasoning. If someone draws a conclusion that fails in even one row that fits the facts, the conclusion doesn't follow. That single row is the proof.

blocks.text: A hallway has two lamps, and each lamp is either on or off. A caretaker has to check the wiring and wants to see the hallway in every possible state before signing it off.

That sounds easy until you try to do it without missing one. With the first lamp on, the second might be on or off. With the first lamp off, the second might again be on or off. It is easy to check three states and feel sure you have seen them all. The caretaker needs a way of listing the states that guarantees nothing is skipped and nothing is counted twice.

Logic has such a list, and this lesson builds it. Each lamp becomes a claim, each state becomes a row, and an extra column says what a sentence like “both lamps are on” comes to in that state. We then use the rows to test a piece of reasoning.

lessons.title: Finding the conclusion

lead.text: Take the doorstep remark again: “You should take an umbrella, because the forecast says rain.” It holds two claims, and they do different jobs. One is what the speaker wants you to accept, that you should take an umbrella. The other is offered to make that easier to accept, that the forecast says rain.

Claims put together like this make an argument. In everyday speech the word often means a quarrel, but in logic it only means reasons given for a claim. The claim the argument is trying to get you to accept is its conclusion. Each claim offered in support of it is a premise. Here the conclusion is that you should take an umbrella, and the one premise is the forecast.

The test for which is which does not depend on the order of the sentences or on how they are built. Ask what the speaker wants you to believe or to do, and the answer is the conclusion. Whatever has been put forward to help is a premise. That test is worth trying on another remark.
Here is a remark with the aim and the reason both in it. Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.
That last remark had a small word in the middle doing quiet work. People leave clues like it all the time, and learning to spot them makes the test from the last screen quicker.

Some words usually lead into a conclusion, such as “so”, “thus” and “hence”. In “The oven is cold, so dinner will be late”, the word “so” points ahead to where the speaker is going. Other words usually lead into a premise, such as “because”, “since” and “given that”. In “I'm taking the bus, because the car won't start”, the word “because” points back to the reason. We can call words like these indicator words.

Indicator words help, but they never settle the matter by themselves. Many arguments carry none at all, and a word like “since” can also mean “ever since”, which has nothing to do with reasons. When the clue is missing or doubtful, go back to asking what the speaker wants you to accept.
“If the battery is charged, the torch lights. The battery is charged. Therefore the torch lights.” Decide the role of the last sentence.

reveal.text: Check your choice against the sentences before it. The first two are premises, and the last is the conclusion they support.

lead.text: So far the conclusion has come last, but it does not have to. Compare two ways of saying the same thing: “The ferry is cancelled, so we'll drive” and “We'll drive, because the ferry is cancelled.” The conclusion, that we'll drive, moves from the end to the front. The premise moves with it from front to back, and the reasoning is the same in both.

That is why position can't be the test. A passage may begin with its conclusion, end with it or tuck it into the middle, and a speaker who has made a point may go on to defend it for several sentences. What stays fixed is the job each claim does. The conclusion is the claim being supported, and a premise is a claim doing the supporting, wherever it appears.
A longer passage shows this better. The next screen works through one, asking at each line what the speaker wants.

blocks.text: The last lesson ended with a table of letters, and nobody talks like that. A friend on your doorstep says, “You should take an umbrella, because the forecast says rain.” A café sign says, “Go early, since the queue is shortest before nine.” Each remark tries to bring you round to something, and each hands you a reason for it.

In ordinary talk the aim and its reason arrive in one breath, and either can come first. Before you can ask whether the reasoning is any good, you have to know which part is which. If you mistake the reason for the aim, you spend your attention checking the wrong sentence.

This lesson takes a few remarks like these apart. It looks for what the speaker is after, then for the clues they leave behind, and it ends by putting one remark back into the letters of the last lesson so that the table can check it.

lessons.title: Valid but untrue

lead.text: Go back to the dragon story and ask the two questions separately. The first is whether the claims are true, and they aren't, since nobody owns a dragon. The second is whether the conclusion would have to be true if the premises were. Here the answer is yes. If every dragon owner is rich and Ana owns a dragon, then Ana is rich, and there is no way to keep the premises and deny the conclusion.

The second question is about the link between the claims, and logic has a word for an argument that passes it. An argument is valid when there is no case in which all its premises are true and its conclusion is false. A case here means a way things could be, like a row of a truth table, and it does not have to be a way things actually are. So validity says nothing about whether the premises hold in the real world.

People often use “valid” to mean “true” or “sensible”, and it means neither. A valid argument is a guarantee about a connection: give it true premises and a true conclusion comes out. It does not supply the true premises.
Think about the guarantee a valid argument gives, and about what it is a guarantee of.

steps.headline: Testing a pattern against the cases

lead.text: Real arguments carry details that have nothing to do with the link, so we test the shape instead, using letters. Take “Lamp 1 is on and lamp 2 is on, so lamp 2 is on.” With p for the first claim and q for the second, it becomes “p ∧ q; therefore q”. A semicolon separates the premises, and here there is only one.

To test a shape, look through the four rows for a bad one. Each row is a possible case, and a bad row is one where every premise is true and the conclusion is false. Only the row TT makes p ∧ q true, and q is true in it. Every other row has a false premise, so none of them can be bad. No bad row exists, so the pattern is valid.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the search skipped every row where a premise was false. Those rows promise nothing, because validity only speaks about cases in which the premises hold. To test a pattern, find the rows where all the premises hold, then check the conclusion in those rows.

lead.text: Test “p → q; p; therefore q” against the four rows. You are looking for a row where both premises are true and q is false.

reveal.text: Compare your answer with the rows. Wherever p → q and p are both true, q is true as well.

steps.headline: A bad row has a name

lead.text: Not every pattern passes the test. Try “p; therefore p ∧ q”, which says that because one lamp is on, both are. The rows where the premise p holds are TT and TF. In TT the conclusion p ∧ q is true, but in TF it is false, so the premise holds and the conclusion fails.

A case like TF has a name. A counterexample to an argument is a case that makes every premise true and the conclusion false. It is the one thing a valid argument cannot have, so validity can be put another way: a valid argument has no counterexamples.
Finding a counterexample is how you show that an argument is invalid. The next example does exactly that, one row at a time.

In FT, p ∨ q and q are true, but the conclusion p is false.
A counterexample exists, so the argument is not valid.

steps.headline: Valid is not the same as true

lead.text: A valid argument can still go wrong, because validity checks the link and leaves the facts alone. The dragon story has a valid link and a false first premise. So does this one: “Every even number is divisible by 4. The number 8 is even. So 8 is divisible by 4.” The first premise is false, since 6 is even and 6 is not divisible by 4. The conclusion is true all the same.

That shows what validity can't do. A valid argument that starts from a false premise gives you no reason to believe its conclusion. Sometimes the conclusion is false, and sometimes, as with the number 8, it comes out true by luck. An argument earns your trust only when both checks pass. A valid argument whose premises are all true is called sound. An argument that fails either check is unsound, and a sound argument always has a true conclusion, because the link carries the truth across.

So the two inspections stay separate. Logic does the first by looking at cases. The second inspection asks whether the premises are true. That is a matter for evidence, and each premise has to be checked on its own.
Soundness asks for two things. Here the argument is described by what it passes and fails, so decide which check it fails.
A learner is judging an argument whose conclusion is plainly false, and blames the reasoning.

blocks.text: A flatmate reads a line from a story aloud: “Everyone who owns a dragon is rich. Ana owns a dragon. So Ana is rich.” The other flatmate groans. “That can't be right. There are no dragons.”

She has a point about the dragons, and yet something in the line holds. Suppose the story were true and a dragon really did sit in Ana's garden. Then the money would follow, and nobody could sensibly say Ana was poor. Two questions have got tangled: whether the story is true, and whether the money follows from it. Plenty of disagreements stall because people answer one when they were asked the other.

This lesson pulls the two questions apart. It builds a way of testing whether one claim follows from others without knowing whether those claims are true, using the rows of the table from earlier. It ends by putting the two tests back together.

lessons.title: Naming the fallacies

lead.text: Start with the neighbour's rule: “If it rains, the street gets wet.” In the words of the if-then lesson, rain is the antecedent, the part after “if”, and a wet street is the consequent, the part after “then”. With p for rain and q for a wet street, the rule is p → q.

The rule is a promise about what rain does. Whenever p is true, q has to be true, so if you learn that it is raining you may safely say the street is getting wet. The arrow runs from rain to wet street. It tells you what follows from rain, and it says nothing about what else might make a street wet, such as a street cleaner or a burst pipe.
So there are two directions to travel along a rule, and the arrow only vouches for one of them. The next question puts the neighbour's step to that test.
Back at the gate: the rule says that rain wets streets, and the street is wet.

The neighbour went against the arrow. A wet street is the consequent, and having found it true, the neighbour concluded that the antecedent was true as well, that it rained. Reasoning that looks as if it works and doesn't is called a fallacy. This one has a name of its own, affirming the consequent, because the second premise asserts, or affirms, the consequent.

Test the pattern the way the last lesson taught, by hunting for a counterexample, a case in which both premises hold and the conclusion fails. A street cleaner supplies one. The rule is true and the street is wet, yet it did not rain. The premises hold and the conclusion is false, so the pattern can lead from truth to falsehood, which makes it invalid.
In letters the pattern is “p → q; q; therefore p”. It treats p → q as though it said q → p, and the lesson on converses showed that those are two different claims.
In letters, p is “It rains” and q is “The street is wet”, so the neighbour's reasoning is “p → q; q; therefore p”.

reveal.text: Compare your choice with the street cleaner's case: the street is wet and it never rained. The premises hold, and the conclusion doesn't.

lead.text: The rule has a second trap. Suppose the morning is dry and someone says, “It didn't rain, so the street is dry.” This time the argument starts from the antecedent being false and concludes that the consequent is false as well. It is called denying the antecedent, because the second premise denies p. The conclusion is ¬q.

The mistake is the same one in a different place. The rule says what happens if it rains. It is silent about what happens if it doesn't, so it leaves the street free to be wet for another reason. The street cleaner serves again: it did not rain, the street is wet and the rule is never broken. The pattern “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q” has a counterexample too.

The two slips mirror each other. One goes from a true consequent back to the antecedent, and the other from a false antecedent forward to a false consequent. Each treats the rule as though it ran in both directions.
Now the second pattern, in the case of the street cleaner: no rain, but a wet street.

Not every way of using a rule goes wrong. Suppose it is dry outside and you want to know whether it rained. The rule says that rain would have left the street wet, and the street is dry. So it did not rain, and you can say so with no doubt at all.

The reason is that the rule promises a wet street if it rained. Suppose it had rained: then the street would be wet, and it isn't. That supposition contradicts what we see, so it has to be rejected. This also moves against the arrow, from the consequent back to the antecedent, but it starts from a false consequent, where the slip started from a true one.

The pattern is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p”, and it is called modus tollens, Latin for the mode that denies. It is valid, and it is the contrapositive from the earlier lesson at work, since ¬q → ¬p says exactly what the original rule says.

steps.headline: Answering the argument, not the person

lead.text: The slips so far are about the shape of the reasoning. There is another kind of slip that has nothing to do with shape, and it is answering the speaker instead of the argument. Suppose someone says, “Their sum must be wrong because they are rude.” Whether a person is rude and whether a sum is right are two separate matters, and the first gives no evidence about the second.

This is called attacking the person. It works in the flattering direction too: “Everyone admires her, so her sum must be right.” In both cases the speaker's manner, popularity or record is treated as though it were a reason. A reason that bears on the conclusion has to be about the sum itself.

To answer an argument, find the step you doubt and test it. You can recheck a calculation, look for a missing premise or search for a counterexample, as we did with the patterns above. If the argument holds up, it holds up whoever says it.

blocks.text: On a grey morning you step outside and find the street wet. A neighbour at the gate says, “If it rains, the street gets wet. The street is wet. So it rained.” It sounds like a tidy bit of reasoning, and most people would nod.

It sounds right, and yet a doubt nags. The street might have been wet for a different reason, and if so the neighbour's rule has been pushed further than it goes. Reasoning of this kind is common because it looks exactly like reasoning that works. The way to catch it is to know the shapes by name.

This lesson names two slips that people make with an if-then rule, and the one safe move that sits beside them. It finishes with a slip of another kind, which is answering the speaker in place of the argument.
