hints: Before the envelope is opened, which verdicts could Mia's claim get?
Is “unknown” a fact about the envelope, or about you?
List the verdicts the envelope itself could make Mia's claim have, then count them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A claim is true or false in a case: two values.

questions.onCorrect: Two. “Unknown” describes what you know, not the claim: the envelope holds the note or it doesn't.

misconceptions.feedback: “Unknown” describes you, not the claim. The envelope already holds what it holds.
A claim can fail as well as hold. Think of Jon's claim when the note is there.

questions.prompt: When p is true, is ¬p true or false?
hints: ¬p says that p is not the case.
If the lamp is on, is “the lamp is not on” correct?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Negation reverses true to false.

questions.onCorrect: False. ¬p makes the opposite claim, so it takes the opposite truth value.

misconceptions.feedback: ¬p says the lamp is not on. Does that match a lamp that is on?

questions.prompt: How should we treat “This painting is beautiful” here?
hints: The speaker is saying how the painting is, even if others disagree.
Does the sentence ask for anything, or tell anyone to do anything?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It asserts an evaluation, so it is a claim, though people dispute it.

questions.onCorrect: It asserts an evaluation, so it is a claim. Disagreement doesn't turn a claim into a question or command.

misconceptions.feedback: Nobody is told to do anything. The speaker says how the painting is.
It asks for nothing. It states a view, which others may dispute.

questions.prompt: Is “Close the window” a claim or a command? Use one word.
hints: Ask whether the sentence says how things are or directs someone to act.
The verb “Close” asks for an action.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It directs an action rather than asserting a truth.

questions.onCorrect: Command. It directs an action; it doesn't say how anything is, so it can't be true or false.

misconceptions.feedback: Could anyone find “Close the window” wrong? It tells someone what to do.

questions.prompt: A claim is false. Is its negation true or false?
hints: Apply negation to the false claim.
Negation never leaves the value alone.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation of a false claim is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. Negation reverses the value, so the negation of a false claim is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Negation never leaves the value alone. Ask what ¬ does to a claim.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q false?
hints: A promise is broken when what was promised does not happen.
Find the case where the code is right but the door stays shut.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The code is correct but the door stays shut: p true, q false.

questions.onCorrect: p true, q false: the code is right and the door stays shut. That is the one case where the promise fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the code is wrong, so the door has made no promise to break.
Here the code is wrong too. The door only promised something about correct codes.

questions.prompt: How many of the four cases make p → q true?
hints: List the four cases: p and q each true or false.
Which one case breaks the promise?
Count the cases that are left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the true–false case is false, so three cases are true.

questions.onCorrect: Three. Only one case breaks the promise, so the other three leave it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of false cases. The question asks for the true ones.
One case does break a promise. Find it and take it away.
Count the cases where p is false as well as those where p is true. Only one case breaks the promise.

questions.prompt: When p and q are both false, is p → q true or false?
hints: With a wrong code, was the door's promise put to the test?
Does this case break the rule?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A false antecedent makes the conditional true.

questions.onCorrect: True. With p false the rule isn't tested, so nothing breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule only promised something about correct codes. Does this case break that?

questions.prompt: Let p mean “The shape is a square” and q mean “The shape has four sides.” Is p → q true or false for a four-sided rectangle that is not a square?
hints: Is p true or false for this shape?
Is this the case where p is true and q is false?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is false for this rectangle, so the rule is not broken: p → q is true.

questions.onCorrect: True. The shape isn't a square, so the rule about squares is untouched. A true q doesn't make p true.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false for this shape. A rule about squares can't be broken by a shape that isn't one.

questions.prompt: p is true and q is false. Is p → q true or false?
hints: Check the case where the antecedent holds but the consequent doesn't.
That case is the one the conditional rules out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its antecedent holds and its consequent fails.

questions.onCorrect: False. The antecedent holds and the consequent fails: the one case that breaks a conditional.

misconceptions.feedback: p holds, so the conditional is being tested. Does q deliver what p promised?

questions.prompt: How many of the four cases make a conditional false?
hints: Go through each combination of p and q.
A false conditional needs p to hold and q to fail.
How many combinations meet both conditions?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Exactly one case is false: true antecedent, false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: One: p true and q false. Every other combination leaves the conditional true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many cases are true. Count the false ones.
A false conditional needs p true and q false together. How many combinations do that?
A broken promise is possible. Find the combination that breaks it.

questions.prompt: Is q → p true or false when q is true and p is false?
hints: In q → p, q is the antecedent and p is the consequent.
Is this the case with a true antecedent and a false consequent?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The converse has a true antecedent and a false consequent.

questions.onCorrect: False. In q → p the antecedent q holds and the consequent p fails. p → q is true in this same case.

misconceptions.feedback: In q → p, q comes first. Apply the rule from the last lesson with q as the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Across the four cases, how many differ between p → q and ¬q → ¬p?
hints: Compare each case of p → q with the same case of ¬q → ¬p.
Negate both inputs and swap their order for the second expression.
Count disagreements, not true cases.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their truth values match in every case, so none differ.

questions.onCorrect: None. The two have the same truth value in every case, so the contrapositive says the same thing.

misconceptions.feedback: The worked example showed the false case: it is false in both. Count the cases where they disagree.
Check each case against the matching one for ¬q → ¬p. They fail in the same case.
They don't disagree everywhere. Compare them case by case.

questions.prompt: Which case makes p → q true but its converse q → p false?
hints: The converse is false only when q is true and p is false.
Check that p → q is still true in that case.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true, p → q is true and q → p is false.

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true. The original holds, the converse fails, so the two are not the same claim.

misconceptions.feedback: Both are true here. You need a case where they disagree.
Here p → q is already false. You need it true.

questions.prompt: Choose the contrapositive of “If fragile, then labelled”.
hints: Swap the two parts, then negate both.
The consequent “labelled” becomes the negated antecedent.

acceptedIdeas: If not labelled, then not fragile
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap and negate both: if not labelled, then not fragile.

choices.label: If not labelled, then not fragile
If not fragile, then not labelled

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if not labelled, then not fragile. It says the same as the original.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but doesn't negate them. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. It isn't the contrapositive.

questions.prompt: What is q → p called relative to p → q?
hints: This swaps the original antecedent and consequent.
It does not negate either claim.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exchanging the two claims gives the converse.

questions.onCorrect: The converse. The parts are swapped and nothing is negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The contrapositive also negates both parts. Here they are only swapped.

questions.prompt: What is ¬q → ¬p called relative to p → q?
hints: This both swaps the order and negates the claims.
Tell it apart from merely swapping p and q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Reversing and negating both claims gives the contrapositive.

questions.onCorrect: The contrapositive. The parts are swapped and both are negated.

misconceptions.feedback: The converse only swaps the parts. Here both are negated as well.

questions.prompt: If Ada is a knight, is Ben a knight or a knave?
hints: A knight's statement must be true.
Apply that to what Ada says about Ben.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A truthful Ada says Ben is a knave, so Ben is a knave.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. A knight's statement is true, so Ada's claim about Ben has to hold.

misconceptions.feedback: Ada says Ben is a knave. If Ada always tells the truth, what does that make Ben?

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” How many assignments of types fit her statement?
hints: Test Ada as a knight, then as a knave.
In each case, which type for Ben makes her statement true if she is a knight, or false if she is a knave?
Count every pair that survives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Either Ada is truthful and Ben a knave, or Ada lies and Ben is a knight.

questions.onCorrect: Two. Ada truthful with Ben a knave, or Ada lying with Ben a knight. One statement can leave several.

misconceptions.feedback: You found one pair. Now assume Ada is a knave, and see whether Ben has a type that fits.
Some of the four pairs make Ada break her own type. Cross those out.
The statement can be made to fit. Try each type for Ada in turn.

questions.prompt: Ada says, “Ben is a knave.” Ben says, “Ada and I are the same type.” Is Ada a knight or a knave?
hints: Only two assignments fit Ada's statement. What are Ada's and Ben's types in each?
In both, are Ada and Ben the same type? Is Ben's statement true or false?
Test Ben as a knight and as a knave against that.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben lies, so Ben is a knave and Ada's claim is true.

questions.onCorrect: Knight. Ben's claim is false in both cases, which makes him a knave and Ada the knight.

misconceptions.feedback: If Ada were a knave, Ben would be a knight. Would Ben's statement then be true?

questions.prompt: Cara says, “Drew is a knight.” Drew says, “Cara is a knave.” How many assignments of types fit both statements?
hints: Try Cara as a knight and check Drew's statement.
Then try Cara as a knave and check whether Drew tells the truth.
Count only assignments in which both speakers obey their own type.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Assuming either type for Cara produces a contradiction, leaving zero assignments.

questions.onCorrect: None. Each type for Cara contradicts Drew's statement, so no assignment survives.

misconceptions.feedback: Check your pair against both statements. Does each speaker obey their own type?
Test each pair against both statements. Both speakers have to obey their type.

questions.prompt: Ada is a knave and says “Ben is a knave.” Is Ben a knight or a knave?
hints: A knave's statement is false.
Reverse Ada's claim about Ben instead of accepting it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ada's claim is false, so Ben is a knight.

questions.onCorrect: Knight. A knave's statement is false, so Ben is not a knave.

misconceptions.feedback: A knave lies. What does that do to what Ada says about Ben?

questions.prompt: How many assignments should you test for two people with two possible types each?
hints: There are two type choices for Ada and two for Ben.
Pair each of Ada's choices with each of Ben's.
Multiply the numbers of choices.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two choices for each person give 2 × 2 = 4 assignments.

questions.onCorrect: Four: 2 × 2. Every choice for Ada pairs with both choices for Ben.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of choices for one person. Pair each of Ada's with each of Ben's.
Pair every one of Ada's choices with every one of Ben's. Count the pairs.

questions.prompt: How many different settings can the two lamps have?
hints: Lamp 1 can be on or off. How many settings is that?
Pair each setting of lamp 1 with both settings of lamp 2.
List them: both on, then the three others.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two settings for one lamp times two for the other gives four.

questions.onCorrect: Four: 2 × 2. Every setting of one lamp pairs with both settings of the other.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the settings of one lamp. The second lamp doubles it.
Check the list. Both lamps on is one setting, so what are the others?

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∧ q true?
hints: The symbol ∧ reads “and”. What does “p and q” need?
Look at TT, TF, FT and FF in turn.
Count only rows with two true inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the TT row makes both claims true.

questions.onCorrect: One. “p and q” needs both, and only the TT row has both.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what you get if one true claim is enough. ∧ needs both.
Check a row with only one claim true. Does “p and q” hold there?
Go through the four rows one at a time and test “p and q”.

questions.prompt: How many rows make p ∨ q true?
hints: Inclusive ∨ needs at least one true input.
Does the row where both are true count?
Which row is the only one that fails?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At least one claim is true in three of the four rows.

questions.onCorrect: Three. “p or q” holds unless both are false, and in this course it includes the row where both are true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many rows make p ∧ q true. Here one true claim is enough.
Rows where both claims are true count too, because ∨ is inclusive.
The row where both claims are false fails.

questions.prompt: Someone reasons: “p or q is true, and p is true, so q must be false.” Which row shows the reasoning goes wrong?
hints: Keep the rows where both starting facts hold.
In one of them q is true. Which?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p and q both true, “p or q” and “p” hold, but q is not false.

questions.onCorrect: p true, q true: both facts hold and q is still true. One such row is enough to break the reasoning.

misconceptions.feedback: p is false here, so one of the starting facts fails. Keep only rows where both hold.
p ∨ q is false here, so this row isn't a case the reasoning starts from.

questions.prompt: Three independent claims each have two truth values. How many rows does the table need?
hints: Each extra claim doubles the number of cases.
Two choices for each of three claims.
Multiply the three numbers of choices.
questions.onCorrect: Eight: 2 × 2 × 2. Each new claim doubles the rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the choices. Each claim multiplies the cases instead.
That is the rows for two claims. The third claim doubles them.

questions.prompt: Can inclusive p ∨ q be true when both claims are true? Answer yes or no.
hints: The word inclusive matters here.
At least one true claim is enough, so both is allowed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction allows both claims to be true.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Inclusive “or” needs at least one claim true, and both counts.

misconceptions.feedback: Inclusive “or” doesn't rule out both. What does “inclusive” add?

questions.prompt: In this argument, is “The torch lights” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: Which statement are the other sentences offered to support?
What does the word “therefore” introduce?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the conclusion supported by the two premises.

questions.onCorrect: Conclusion. The first two sentences are the support, and “therefore” introduces what they support.

misconceptions.feedback: A premise is offered as support. Is “The torch lights” offered to support something, or supported?

questions.prompt: How many rows make both p → q and p true?
hints: First keep the rows with p true.
Of those, drop any row where p → q is false.
Count the rows that satisfy both premises at once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only TT makes both premises true.

questions.onCorrect: One. Only TT makes both premises true, and q is true in that row.

misconceptions.feedback: Two rows have p true. Is p → q true in both?
Both premises have to hold in the same row. Test p first.
Go through the four rows and test both premises in each.

questions.prompt: “The torch lights, because the battery is charged and a charged battery makes it light.” In this passage, is “The battery is charged” a premise or a conclusion?
hints: A sentence's role depends on what it supports, not where it sits.
What is the charged battery offered as a reason for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It supplies support, so it is a premise.

questions.onCorrect: Premise. It is offered as a reason for the torch lighting, though it comes later in the passage.

misconceptions.feedback: The passage starts with its conclusion. Is the battery being charged what the speaker wants you to accept, or a reason for it?

questions.prompt: “Either the parcel is at the desk or it is in the locker. It is not at the desk. Therefore it is in the locker.” Which location is the conclusion: desk or locker?
hints: Which sentence follows “therefore”?
The first two sentences support that one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “Therefore” introduces the locker claim.

questions.onCorrect: Locker. “Therefore” introduces it, and the two earlier claims support it.

misconceptions.feedback: The desk appears in the premises. Which claim comes after “therefore”?

questions.prompt: What do we call a claim offered as support for a conclusion?
hints: This is the supporting part of an argument.
Tell the evidence apart from the claim it is meant to establish.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A premise is offered in support of the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: A premise. It supports the conclusion; it is not what the argument wants you to accept.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is what the support is for. What is the support called?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?
hints: Look at the statement after “therefore”.
The two earlier statements support that letter.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is q.

questions.onCorrect: q. It follows “therefore”, and the two earlier statements are offered as its support.

misconceptions.feedback: p appears in the premises. Which letter follows “therefore”?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Ask whether both premises can be true while q is false.
The first premise links p to q, and the second states p.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No row makes both premises true and q false.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. In every row where both premises hold, q holds too.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where both premises are true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: How many counterexamples may a valid argument have?
hints: Validity says no case has true premises and a false conclusion.
What does the definition allow for such cases?
Count the exceptions it permits.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A single counterexample would make it invalid, so a valid argument has none.

questions.onCorrect: None. One counterexample would make the argument invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: One counterexample is enough to make an argument invalid. How many does validity permit?
Validity is a guarantee over every case. How many exceptions does that allow?

questions.prompt: Is the argument “p → q; q; therefore p” valid or invalid?
hints: Look for a row where p → q and q are both true.
Of those rows, check whether the conclusion p is true in every one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The false–true row is a counterexample.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. With p false and q true, both premises hold and the conclusion fails.

misconceptions.feedback: Test the row with p false and q true. Do both premises hold, and what happens to p?

questions.prompt: A valid argument contains a false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Soundness needs two things: validity and true premises.
Does the stated premise meet the second?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Soundness requires validity and all true premises.

questions.onCorrect: Unsound. Soundness needs every premise to be true as well as validity.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity alone isn't enough. What does soundness also ask of the premises?

questions.prompt: A valid argument has all true premises. Is it sound or unsound?
hints: Recall both parts of the definition of soundness.
The question gives you validity and true premises.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It meets both requirements for soundness.

questions.onCorrect: Sound. It is valid and every premise is true.

misconceptions.feedback: Soundness needs validity and true premises. Does this argument have both?

questions.prompt: How many true-premise, false-conclusion cases are needed to refute validity?
hints: Validity says there are no cases with true premises and a false conclusion.
One exception breaks a promise about every case.
You don't need most of the table to be counterexamples.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One counterexample disproves the guarantee.

questions.onCorrect: One. A single case with true premises and a false conclusion refutes validity.

misconceptions.feedback: With no such case, the argument is valid. How many are needed to refute it?
You don't need several. Validity promises there are none.

questions.prompt: Which case refutes “p → q; q; therefore p”?
hints: Both premises must stay true, so keep p → q true and q true.
To refute the conclusion p, make p false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With p false and q true both premises hold and the conclusion p fails.

questions.onCorrect: p false, q true: both premises hold and p is false. A true consequent doesn't establish its antecedent.

misconceptions.feedback: Here p is true, so the conclusion holds. You need a case where it fails.
Here q is false, so a premise fails. Keep both premises true.

questions.prompt: Take p false and q true in “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”. Is the conclusion ¬q true or false?
hints: The conclusion is ¬q, not q.
Apply negation to q = true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion ¬q is false because q is true.

questions.onCorrect: False. Both premises hold but ¬q fails, so denying the antecedent is invalid.

misconceptions.feedback: The conclusion is ¬q, and q is true here. What does negation do to it?

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid?
hints: Suppose p were true while q is false.
Would that satisfy the first premise p → q?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both premises force p false, so ¬p follows.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. If p were true, p → q would force q, but ¬q says otherwise. This is modus tollens.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p → q and ¬q are true and ¬p is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: Someone argues, “Their calculation must be wrong because they are rude.” Which response examines the reasoning?
hints: Rudeness says nothing about the sums.
Choose the response that looks at the step or the evidence.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Checking the disputed step addresses the reasoning. Manners don't settle it.

choices.label: Treat the speaker's popularity as proof

questions.onCorrect: Check the step itself. Rudeness doesn't make a calculation right or wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: That attacks the person again. It doesn't test the calculation.
Popularity is not evidence about the calculation either.

questions.prompt: In “p → q; q; therefore p”, which part is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: In p → q, p comes before the arrow and q after it.
The second premise asserts q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: q is the consequent, which the argument affirms.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts q, the part after the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is p, before the arrow. Which letter does the second premise assert?

questions.prompt: In “p → q; ¬p; therefore ¬q”, which part is denied: antecedent or consequent?
hints: Which part of p → q does p stand for?
The second premise ¬p denies that part.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is the antecedent, which the argument denies.

questions.onCorrect: Antecedent. ¬p denies p, the part before the arrow.

misconceptions.feedback: The consequent is q. The second premise denies p. Which part is that?

questions.prompt: Why do we throw away the rows where p is true?
hints: Which facts did we start with?

acceptedIdeas: We were told p is not true, so those rows don't fit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: We know p is not true, so the rows where p is true don't match what we know.

choices.label: We were told p is not true, so those rows don't fit.
p ∨ q is false in those rows.
Rows with p true are always wrong.

questions.onCorrect: The rows must match everything we know. We know p is not true, so those rows are out.

misconceptions.feedback: Check TT and TF. Is p ∨ q false there?
A row with p true is fine in general. It just doesn't match what we were told here.

questions.prompt: An alarm rings if sensor p or sensor q is triggered. Of the four settings of the two sensors, how many leave the alarm silent?
hints: The alarm follows p ∨ q. When does it fail to ring?
Which of the four settings has neither sensor triggered?
Count the rows where p ∨ q is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: p ∨ q is false only when both are false, so one setting.

questions.onCorrect: One: neither sensor triggered. “p or q” fails only when both are false.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many settings ring the alarm. Count the silent ones.
A setting with one sensor triggered still rings the alarm.
Go through the four settings one at a time and check the alarm.

questions.prompt: Which list is a complete table for two claims?
hints: Each claim can be true or false, and every pairing needs a row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every pairing appears once: TT, TF, FT, FF.

questions.onCorrect: Every pairing of true and false appears exactly once, so the table is complete.

misconceptions.feedback: One pairing is missing. Pair each value of p with both values of q.
One row appears twice, and another pairing is missing.

questions.prompt: A café sign says “Tea or coffee included.” Dev takes both. In the logician's sense, is the sign's claim true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Does the symbol ∨ rule out the case where both hold?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The logician's “or” allows both.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. In logic “or” includes both, so taking both still makes it true.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the everyday reading. The logician's “or” doesn't rule out both.

questions.prompt: Is the file encrypted?
hints: The rule says what encrypted files need. Does it say only encrypted files need one?
Could a file need a key for some other reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Not necessarily. Other files may need a key too.

questions.onCorrect: Not necessarily. “If encrypted, then key” doesn't say that a key means encrypted. Turning a rule round changes it.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what encrypted files need. It doesn't say that only encrypted files need one.
The rule doesn't rule encryption out. It just doesn't settle it.

questions.prompt: Why is ¬q → ¬p false in this row?
hints: Work out ¬q and ¬p for this row first.
What makes any conditional false?

acceptedIdeas: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ¬q is true and ¬p is false, which is the one case that breaks a conditional.

choices.label: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: a true antecedent with a false consequent.
Swapping the parts never changes a conditional.
A negated claim is always false.

questions.onCorrect: ¬q is true and ¬p is false: the same broken-promise pattern, reached by negating and swapping.

misconceptions.feedback: Swapping alone does change a conditional. That is why the converse differs. Look at ¬q and ¬p.
¬ flips a value. It doesn't fix it.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If it's a square, it has four sides.” A shape does not have four sides. What follows?
hints: Write the contrapositive of the rule first.
The contrapositive starts from “not four sides”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive says: if it doesn't have four sides, it isn't a square.

questions.onCorrect: Not a square. The contrapositive says the same as the rule: no four sides, so not a square.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs against the rule: squares have four sides.
The rule's contrapositive starts from exactly this fact.

questions.prompt: What is the converse of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: The converse swaps the two parts and negates nothing.

acceptedIdeas: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap the parts: if the match is cancelled, it rains.

choices.label: If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.
If it rains, the match is played.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate nothing: if the match is cancelled, it rains.

misconceptions.feedback: That negates both parts but keeps the order. The converse only swaps.
That keeps the order and negates one part. The converse only swaps the parts.

questions.prompt: What is the contrapositive of “If it rains, the match is cancelled”?
hints: Swap the parts, then negate both.

acceptedIdeas: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Swap and negate both parts: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

choices.label: If the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.
If the match is cancelled, it rains.
If it doesn't rain, the match isn't cancelled.

questions.onCorrect: Swap the parts and negate both: if the match isn't cancelled, it isn't raining.

misconceptions.feedback: That swaps the parts but negates neither. It is the converse.
That negates both parts but keeps the order. The contrapositive also swaps them.

questions.prompt: Which claim is Sam trying to get you to accept: the umbrella or the forecast? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim is the reason, and which is the thing the reason is for?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sam wants you to take an umbrella. The forecast is the reason given.

questions.onCorrect: Taking an umbrella is what Sam wants. The forecast is offered as the reason.

misconceptions.feedback: Sam gives the forecast as a reason. What is it a reason for?

questions.prompt: “It will rain, so the match is off.” Which claim is the conclusion: the rain or the match? Answer with one word.
hints: Which claim is offered as the reason for the other?
Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “So” points to the conclusion: the match is off.

questions.onCorrect: The match is off. The rain is the reason given, and it is meant to support the match being off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reason given. What does it support?

questions.prompt: Why isn't “the last train is at nine” the conclusion, even though it comes last?
hints: Ask what the speaker wants you to accept.

acceptedIdeas: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Position doesn't decide. The train time is offered as a reason to leave.

choices.label: Position doesn't decide; it supports the claim that we must leave.
The last sentence is never a conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Where a claim sits doesn't decide its role. It is a premise because it supports the claim that we must leave.

misconceptions.feedback: A conclusion can come last. Here it just doesn't.
“Because” introduces a reason, the premise.

questions.prompt: “Since the shop is shut on Sundays and today is Sunday, you can't buy bread today.” Which claim is the conclusion?
hints: “Since” introduces reasons.
Which claim do the other two support?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two “since” claims support that you can't buy bread today.

choices.label: The shop is shut on Sundays.

questions.onCorrect: You can't buy bread today. “Since” introduces the two premises that support it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a reason offered after “since”. What does it help to support?
That follows “since”, so it is a reason. Which claim does it support?

questions.prompt: Did Sam break his promise? Answer yes or no.
hints: Who was the promise about: people who passed, or people who failed?
What would Sam have to do to be caught out?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The promise only covered the case where you passed.

questions.onCorrect: No. Sam only promised something about passing. A kind act in another case can't break it.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at what the promise covers. Is it about people who failed?

questions.prompt: In “If the code is correct, the door opens”, which part is the antecedent?
hints: The antecedent is the part after “if”.
The consequent is the part after “then”.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The antecedent follows “if”: the code is correct.

questions.onCorrect: The part after “if” is the antecedent. The part after “then” is the consequent.

misconceptions.feedback: That part comes after “then”. It is the consequent, not the antecedent.
The antecedent is one part of the sentence, the part that sets the condition.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the match being cancelled without rain break the promise?
hints: Read the promise again. Which days does it cover?

acceptedIdeas: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The promise only speaks about rainy days, so a dry day can't break it.

choices.label: The promise only speaks about rainy days.
A cancelled match always keeps a promise.

questions.onCorrect: The promise covers only rainy days. On a dry day it says nothing, so it can't be broken.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule doesn't say rain is the only cause, or even a cause. It says what follows when it rains.
A cancelled match keeps this promise only on a rainy day. Dry days are not covered at all.

questions.prompt: The rule is “If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.” Which number would break it?
hints: A rule breaks only when its first part holds and its second part fails.
Test each number against both parts of the rule.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None of them. To break the rule a number would have to be divisible by 4 and odd.

questions.onCorrect: None. Breaking the rule needs a multiple of 4 that is odd, and 8 is divisible by 4 and even.

misconceptions.feedback: 6 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule says nothing about it.
7 isn't divisible by 4, so the rule has no say about it.
8 is divisible by 4. Is it also even?

questions.prompt: Why is “Eli a knave, Fay a knight” ruled out?
hints: Check what Fay says about Eli in this case.
A knight's statement must be true.

acceptedIdeas: Fay is a knight, but her statement about Eli is false.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fay is a knight, so her statement must be true. Eli is a knave, so “Eli is a knight” is false.

choices.label: Fay is a knight, but her statement about Eli is false.
Knaves can't appear in a pair.
Fay's statement is true, which a knight can't say.

questions.onCorrect: A knight's statement has to be true. Here Fay's is false, so the case breaks a rule.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing stops a knave from being in a pair. Check each person's statement against their type.
Knights are supposed to say true things. Check whether Fay's statement is true here.

questions.prompt: Gus says, “Hal is a knight.” Hal says, “Gus and I are different types.” Is Gus a knight or a knave?
hints: List the four pairs of types for Gus and Hal.
For each pair, check both statements against the types.
Which pair has nobody breaking their type?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only both being knaves fits both statements, so Gus is a knave.

questions.onCorrect: Knave. Only one pair survives: both knaves, where each statement is false as it must be.

misconceptions.feedback: If Gus were a knight, Hal would be a knight and Hal's statement would have to be true. Is it?

questions.prompt: A knave says, “It is raining.” Is that claim true or false?
hints: What does a knave always do?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A knave always lies, so the claim is false.

questions.onCorrect: A knave always lies, so whatever a knave claims is false.

misconceptions.feedback: That's what a knight's statement would be. What does a knave do?

questions.prompt: Does the street being wet prove that it rained? Answer yes or no.
hints: The rule says what rain does. Does it say rain is the only way?
Could a street be wet for another reason?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Something else could have wet the street.

questions.onCorrect: No. The rule says rain wets the street. It doesn't say nothing else does.

misconceptions.feedback: Rain is one way to get a wet street. Does the rule say it is the only way?

questions.prompt: “If the sensor overheats, the light turns on. The light is on, so the sensor overheated.” Which part of the conditional is affirmed: antecedent or consequent?
hints: The antecedent follows “if”, and the consequent follows “then”.
Which part does the second sentence assert?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The light being on is the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Consequent. The argument asserts the “then” part and argues back to the “if” part.

misconceptions.feedback: The antecedent is the “if” part, the overheating. The second sentence asserts the light being on.

questions.prompt: Why does the light being off show the sensor didn't overheat?
hints: Suppose it had overheated. What would the rule say about the light?

acceptedIdeas: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: If it had overheated, the light would be on. It isn't, so it didn't.

choices.label: Overheating would have turned the light on, and it didn't.
The light is only on when nothing overheats.
Sensors that don't overheat keep their lights off.

questions.onCorrect: Overheating would have turned the light on. It is off, so the sensor didn't overheat.

misconceptions.feedback: That reverses the rule. It says what overheating does to the light.
The rule doesn't say that. It says what overheating does, not what happens without it.

questions.prompt: “If it's a bird, it has feathers. This animal has feathers, so it's a bird.” Is this reasoning valid or invalid?
hints: Which part of the rule does the second sentence assert?
Is there a way to have the feathers without being a bird?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Other animals could have feathers too. It affirms the consequent.

questions.onCorrect: Invalid. It affirms the consequent: feathers could come from another source, so the rule doesn't give the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule says what birds have. Does it say only birds have feathers?

questions.prompt: If the first two sentences were true, would Ana have to be rich? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the first two sentences are true. What follows about Ana?
Ignore whether dragons exist.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A dragon owner is rich, and Ana owns one.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. If the premises held, Ana would have to be rich. Whether they hold is a separate question.

misconceptions.feedback: Suppose the first two sentences are true, whatever the real world is like. Could Ana avoid being rich?

questions.prompt: All the premises of a valid argument are true. Must its conclusion be true? Answer yes or no.
hints: Is there any case with true premises and a false conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: A valid argument has no case with true premises and a false conclusion. What does that leave?

questions.prompt: Why is one counterexample enough to show an argument invalid?
hints: What does validity promise about cases?

acceptedIdeas: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validity promises no case with true premises and a false conclusion. One is enough to break it.

choices.label: Validity promises there is no such case, and one case breaks the promise.
Most of the rows have to be counterexamples.
The premises are false in all the other rows.

questions.onCorrect: Validity is a promise about every case, so a single exception breaks it.

misconceptions.feedback: Validity allows no such case at all. It is not a matter of how many.
The other rows don't matter. Validity is about cases with true premises.

questions.prompt: “All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly.” A learner says: “It's invalid, because the conclusion is false.” Is the learner right? Answer yes or no.
hints: Imagine the premises are true. Could the conclusion still be false?
Is a false conclusion the same as an invalid argument?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. If the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be. The argument is valid but unsound.

questions.onCorrect: No. The conclusion follows from the premises, so it is valid. The first premise is false, so it is unsound.

misconceptions.feedback: A false conclusion doesn't make an argument invalid. Ask whether true premises would force it.

questions.prompt: Is the pattern “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q” valid or invalid?
hints: Find the rows where both premises are true.
Is q true in every one of them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the row with p false and q true keeps both premises true, and q is true there.

questions.onCorrect: Valid. The only row where both premises hold is FT, and q is true there.

misconceptions.feedback: Look for a row where p ∨ q and ¬p are both true and q is false. Is there one?

questions.prompt: Who is right?
hints: Could the envelope hold a £10 note and not hold one?
Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. Does it change what is inside?

acceptedIdeas: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Exactly one of them. The envelope already holds a note or it doesn't.

choices.label: Exactly one of them, but we don't know which yet.

questions.onCorrect: One of them is right already. Not knowing which is a gap in us, not in the envelope. Logic starts there.

misconceptions.feedback: Opening the envelope finds out what is inside. It doesn't decide it.
Mia says the note is there and Jon says it isn't. The envelope can't match both.

questions.prompt: A jar holds some sweets and nobody has counted them. How many truth values does “The jar holds an even number of sweets” have right now?
hints: Does the jar hold some number of sweets right now?
Even or odd is already settled by what is in the jar.
In one case, how many verdicts does a claim get?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The jar holds some number, so the claim has already one value, even though no one knows it.

questions.onCorrect: One. The jar's contents settle it, whether or not anyone counts. Not knowing doesn't remove the value.

misconceptions.feedback: Not counting doesn't remove the verdict. The jar already holds some number.
Two verdicts exist, but the contents of the jar have already settled which applies.
“Unknown” describes the counter, not the claim.

questions.prompt: Nobody has opened the envelope. What does that tell us about Mia's claim?
hints: Does opening the envelope change what is inside it?

acceptedIdeas: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has a truth value.

choices.label: It has a truth value already; we just haven't found it out.
It has no truth value until someone looks.

questions.onCorrect: The envelope already holds what it holds, so the claim already has its truth value.

misconceptions.feedback: Looking finds out what is there. It doesn't put it there.
“Unknown” describes what we know. The claim is checked against the envelope, not against us.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the negation of “The door is open”?
hints: The negation claims that the original fails.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: “The door is not open” says the original claim fails.

questions.onCorrect: The negation says the original fails: the door is not open.

misconceptions.feedback: That agrees with the original, with more emphasis. A negation says the original fails.
That asks. It doesn't claim that the original fails.

flashcards.front: When p is false, what truth value does ¬p have?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The negation is true.

flashcards.front: What kind of sentence is “Where is the key?”: claim, question or command?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a question.

flashcards.front: When is p → q false? Answer with the two values in order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: p is true and q is false.

flashcards.front: Is p → q true or false when p is false and q is true?
flashcards.back: True: the rule is not broken.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The material conditional is true.

flashcards.front: Name the equivalent transformation of p → q.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The contrapositive is equivalent.

flashcards.front: How many assignments distinguish a conditional from its contrapositive?
flashcards.back: Zero: they agree on every assignment.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: They differ on zero assignments.

flashcards.front: How many type assignments are possible for two islanders before any claims are checked?
flashcards.back: Four assignments: each islander has two possible types.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two times two gives four assignments.

flashcards.front: A knave says “Eli is a knight.” What is Eli’s type?
flashcards.back: Eli is a knave because the statement is false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Eli must be a knave.

flashcards.front: How many rows does a complete truth table for four independent claims need?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four independent claims require sixteen assignments.

flashcards.front: When p and q are both true, is inclusive p ∨ q true or false?
flashcards.back: True: at least one is true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Inclusive disjunction is true.

flashcards.front: What is a claim offered as support in an argument called?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is a premise.

flashcards.front: For “p ∨ q; ¬p; therefore q”, which letter is the conclusion?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The conclusion is q.

flashcards.front: A valid argument has one false premise. Is it sound or unsound?
flashcards.back: Unsound: soundness requires every premise to be true.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The argument is unsound.

flashcards.front: How many counterexamples are compatible with validity?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Validity permits zero counterexamples.

flashcards.front: “p → q; q; therefore p” affirms which part of the conditional?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It affirms the consequent.

flashcards.front: Is “p → q; ¬q; therefore ¬p” valid or invalid?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The inference is valid.
